summary: Discusses how IETF working groups typically handle the documents they work on. It focuses on the common practice of adopting an existing draft as a starting point, which may be anything from a widely used specification to a blank sheet. It is informational guidance, not a formal process rule.

plainLanguage.summary: A club wants to write a rulebook. This document explains the usual ways they pick a first draft to start from and then keep improving it together.

questions: how do ietf working groups adopt drafts
how are internet-drafts handled in a working group
can a working group create a draft from scratch
subtitle: How working groups develop and adopt documents through consensus

tldr.problem: IETF working groups need guidance on how to formally adopt and develop Internet-Drafts, which can start from widely used specs, blank pages, or anywhere in between.
tldr.mechanism: Working groups follow a common adoption sequence, check for IPR issues, select editors, and ensure rough consensus drives all significant changes to documents.
tldr.outcome: This informational guide explains the typical practices but is not a formal requirement, leaving flexibility for each working group to choose its process within IETF constraints.

today: RFC 7221 is an informational guide to working group practices and remains the reference for how IETF groups typically handle document adoption and development. It is not a normative process requirement but reflects consensus practice.

sections.title: What Is a Working Group Draft
sections.content:
An IETF working group draft is an Internet-Draft (I-D) that belongs to a working group and is subject to the working group's revision control. Working groups identify their official drafts with the filename pattern draft-ietf-wgname-..., distinguishing them from individual submissions like draft-lastname-.... The creation of a working group draft or any major change to it requires rough consensus within the working group.

Working groups use I-Ds as their mechanism for producing official output, as mandated by their charter. The document an adopted I-D started as can range from a widely deployed specification, to a blank sheet wholly created by the group, to anything in between. Responsibility for editing falls to document authors and editors selected by the working group Chairs.
sections.plainLanguage: A working group draft is an official document the group owns and controls together. Its filename shows it belongs to the group, not to any single person. Everyone can change it, but only if the group agrees.

sections.title: Working Group Authority and Consensus
sections.content:
The IETF premise is clear: within a working group, the working group itself has final authority over document content, within the constraints of the charter. Individual Chairs, authors and editors have no special authority. The process uses rough consensus—approximate but clear and strong agreement—rather than requiring unanimity.

For difficult topics and contentious working group dynamics, explicit rough consensus processes are essential to validate progress at each step. For simpler matters, working groups often use efficiency modes, such as allowing a Chair to assert likely agreement and call for objections. The mode of decision-making is chosen by the comfort and engagement of the group itself.

When the opinion of the working group is unclear, Chairs can poll the group. The form of the question matters: asking supporters and detractors to provide reasons, not just preferences, treats consensus as ongoing discussion and can produce both document and view changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The group, not the boss, makes the final decision. They do not all need to agree perfectly, just strongly enough. When it is unclear, they ask people what they think.

sections.title: The Adoption Sequence
sections.content:
When a working group wants to adopt a document, Chairs typically follow a common sequence. First, they remind the current draft owners that change control transfers to the IETF—a significant point if proprietary interests are involved. Then, they check for known Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) issues that need disclosure. Once rough consensus is obtained from the group, the Chairs select document editors, and the authors post the new working group version. The non-working-group version is marked as replaced by this working group version.

No formal specification for adoption exists in IETF procedure documents; this RFC describes the common practice. Basic considerations for adoption include scope within the working group charter, clarity of purpose, whether the draft provides an acceptable platform for continued effort, any process or technical objections, likelihood of timely completion, reasonable intended status, and strong working group support.

Adoption requires rough consensus, not unanimity. The draft's writing quality need not be publication-ready on adoption, though it should be checked. Adoption is initial, not final: the document need not already contain a complete solution. Adoption also does not guarantee publication as an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The group follows a checklist: move ownership to the IETF, check for patent problems, get everyone to agree, pick someone to edit it, post it, and mark the old version as replaced. Nobody needs to think it is perfect yet.

sections.title: Authors, Editors, and Document Stability
sections.content:
Document authors and editors are chosen solely by the Working Group Chairs, though the views of the working group should be considered. They are responsible for incorporating working group consensus into the document. The distinction between author and editor is subjective: a rule of thumb is that editors tend to do the mechanics of incorporating group detail, while authors tend to create detail subject to group approval.

When a working group adopts an existing document, there is a special challenge: selecting whether to keep the original editors or choose new ones. The IETF working group process can differ markedly from the process that created previous versions, so new editors may be appropriate. If original editors continue, the Chairs should ensure they understand IETF working group process.

Within its charter, a working group is free to create new documents from scratch. The criteria for adopting existing drafts are the same as for brand-new documents; working groups sometimes form design teams to produce the first version of a working group draft. A working group is not obligated to retain documents once adopted; if the group concludes a draft is no longer appropriate, anyone can pursue it as an individual or independent submission.
sections.plainLanguage: The chairs pick the people who will do the writing, but the group keeps them honest. If a document changes hands, new writers might understand the group's way better. A group can also drop a document and let someone else pursue it.

sections.title: Handling Special Cases
sections.content:
Individual I-Ds under group care: A working group can facilitate an individual draft without owning it. These documents use the naming convention draft-<lastname>-<wgname>... and remain under author control, though the group can apply normal process management. Ownership and approval are negotiated with the document authors, working group, and Area Directors. This is rare; Area Directors will want to understand why the group could not adopt and own the document.

Competing drafts: Engineering on interesting topics often produces competing proposals due to technical aesthetics, trade-offs, architecture, or economics. A working group is free to pursue more than one proposal. It is appealing to ask competing authors to merge their work. A design team is often better for detailed merger discussions than an open mailing list, but some differences cannot be resolved and merging may produce a weaker result. The working group has ultimate authority. Useful techniques include developing a requirements document independent of specific proposals, building a comparison table of the proposals, and discussing the relative value of one versus multiple proposals.

WG drafts becoming individual: A working group is not obligated to retain documents it has adopted. Sometimes a working group concludes that a draft is no longer appropriate for working group effort. When the working group drops a draft, anyone is permitted to pursue it as an individual or independent submission, subject to existing copyright constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: A group can help with a draft without owning it. If two good ideas compete, the group can keep both or help the authors merge them. A group can also abandon a draft and let someone else take it.
